groups.context:
A green roof is a rooftop that is partly or completely covered with living plants. Beneath the plants lie several layers: soil or a lighter growing material, a drainage layer, and a waterproof sheet that protects the building. Grass-covered roofs are centuries old, but the modern version was developed in Germany in the second half of the twentieth century and has since spread worldwide.

The benefits are considerable. During a storm, the soil and plants hold much of the rain and release it slowly, which reduces the pressure on city drains and lowers the risk of flooded streets. In summer, a planted roof stays far cooler than a dark conventional one, so the rooms below need less air conditioning. Green roofs also offer food and shelter to insects and birds in neighborhoods with little open land.

Nevertheless, green roofs are not suitable everywhere. Wet soil is heavy, and many older buildings would have to be strengthened before they could carry it. A green roof also costs more to install than an ordinary one, and its plants need occasional care. For these reasons, some cities offer tax reductions or direct payments to owners who install them, while others require them on large new buildings. Supporters argue that the long-term savings outweigh the initial expense.

groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
The human brain is an expensive organ. Although it makes up only about two percent of body weight, it consumes roughly a fifth of the energy the body uses at rest. How our ancestors managed to feed such a demanding organ is a long-standing puzzle. One influential answer, proposed by the primatologist Richard Wrangham, is that they learned to cook.

Heat softens food and begins to break it down before it is eaten. As a result, the body obtains more energy from a cooked meal than from the same meal raw and spends less effort chewing and digesting it. Wild chimpanzees spend several hours a day simply chewing. According to Wrangham, cooking freed early humans from this burden, and the surplus energy allowed the brain to expand. He links the change to Homo erectus, a species that appeared nearly two million years ago with smaller teeth and a larger brain than its predecessors.

Skeptics point to a gap in the record. Clear traces of controlled fire, such as hearths, are much younger than the first Homo erectus fossils. Some researchers therefore credit other changes, including eating more meat or pounding food with stone tools, for the early growth of the brain. The debate remains open, yet few doubt that cooking, whenever it began, reshaped the human body.

options: A change in how cars were put together

listening.script: Let's start with a number. Before nineteen thirteen, it took workers at Henry Ford's factory more than twelve hours to assemble the chassis of one Model T, that's the frame with the engine and wheels. About a year later, it took an hour and a half. What changed? Not the car. What changed was how the work moved. Before, the car stayed in one place, and teams of workers walked around it, fetching parts. Ford's engineers turned that around. They put the car on a moving line and had it travel past the workers. Each person stood in one spot and did one small job, over and over, maybe tightening the same two bolts all day. The results were dramatic. Because cars were faster to build, they were cheaper to build, and the price of a Model T fell year after year, until ordinary families could afford one. But there was a cost. The work was so dull and so tiring that workers kept quitting, and Ford had to keep hiring and training new ones. His answer, in nineteen fourteen, was the five-dollar day, roughly double the usual pay. It worked. People stayed. And, as it happened, with wages like that, his own workers could now buy the cars they were building.

listening.script: Here's something that ought to puzzle us more than it does. Nobody sits a two-year-old down and explains the past tense. And yet, by four or so, virtually every child is using it. So how do they pull that off? The obvious guess is imitation. Children just copy what they hear. But listen to the mistakes they make. A child will say 'I goed to the park' or 'two foots.' Now, no adult says 'goed.' The child can't be copying. What she's done is work out a rule, put a 'd' sound on the end for the past, and apply it a little too enthusiastically. There's a lovely experiment from the nineteen fifties that makes the same point. The researcher, Jean Berko, showed young children a drawing of an imaginary creature and said, 'This is a wug.' Then she showed them two. 'Now there are two...' And the children said 'wugs.' They'd never heard that word in their lives, so they couldn't have memorized its plural. And interestingly, when parents do correct their children, it tends to be about facts, not grammar. Call a dog a cat, and you'll be corrected. Say something true in broken grammar, and you'll get a smile. So children aren't parrots. They're more like little scientists, testing guesses about a system no one has explained to them.

Dear Professor Lindqvist,

groups.instructions: Your professor is teaching a class on education policy. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

professor.name: Dr. Moreau
professor.post: This week, we are examining how universities design their degree programs. At many universities, students must complete general education courses in fields unrelated to their major, so an engineering student may have to study literature and a history student may have to take a science class. Some educators see this as essential to a complete education, whereas others consider it a waste of students' time and money. What is your view? Should universities require every student to take courses outside their major? Why or why not?

students.name: Lucas
students.post: I support the requirement. Most of us chose our majors at eighteen, before we had tried many subjects. A required course in another field can reveal an interest we never knew we had. My cousin started in accounting, took a required geology class, and ended up changing her major. Without that rule, she would never have found the career she loves.

students.name: Yuna
students.post: I see it differently. University is already expensive, and every required course outside my major costs money and delays the classes I actually need for my career. If I want to learn about art or history, I can read books or watch free lectures online. Universities should let adults decide how to spend their own time and tuition.

questions.prompt: Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

In my view, universities should keep a requirement for courses outside the major, but it should be small and flexible. I understand Yuna's concern about cost; nobody wants to pay for classes that feel irrelevant. However, I think she overlooks how much working life changes. Many graduates end up in jobs that did not exist when they started their degrees, and they need skills from several fields to adapt. A programmer who has studied psychology, for example, can design software that people actually enjoy using. Lucas mentions discovering new interests, and I would add that mixed classes also teach students to work with people who think differently from them. To limit the cost, universities could require only three or four such courses and let students choose freely among them. That way, the requirement broadens students' education without holding them back.

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 1 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: On a normal weekday, I go to bed at around half past eleven and get up at seven, so I sleep for about seven and a half hours. In the last hour before bed, I try to follow the same routine. First, I prepare my bag and my clothes for the next morning so that I don't have to rush. Then I take a warm shower and read a few pages of a novel. I have to admit that I often look at my phone as well, even though I know it keeps me awake longer. On weekends, I go to bed much later and sleep until nine or ten.

listening.script: Thank you for joining me today. To start, I'd like to hear about a typical night. What time do you usually go to bed and get up, and what do you do in the last hour before you sleep?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 2 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I am definitely a morning person. My mind is clearest between about seven and eleven, so I plan my day around those hours. I do the tasks that need the most concentration, such as writing essays or solving math problems, before lunch. In the afternoon, I feel slower, so I use that time for easier things like answering messages, shopping, or going to the gym. By ten at night, I can hardly keep my eyes open, and anything I study then, I forget by the next day. My friends who are night owls think this is strange, but getting up early suits me.

listening.script: Some people do their best work early in the morning, while others feel more awake late at night. Which kind of person are you, and how does that affect the way you plan your day?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 3 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I mostly agree. Many students I know take their phones to bed and plan to check one message, but then they keep watching videos for an hour. The content never ends, so it is hard to stop. Messages also arrive late at night, and people feel they must reply at once. However, I don't think phones are the only cause. Students also lose sleep because of homework, part-time jobs, and early classes. Even without a phone, a student who finishes work at eleven and has a class at eight will be tired. So phones make the problem worse, but they did not create it.

listening.script: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people say that students today do not get enough sleep because of smartphones and social media. Do you agree? Why or why not?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 4 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: Yes, I think more schools should start later, at least for teenagers. When I was in high school, my first class began at half past seven, and most of us were half asleep. We did not learn much in that first hour, so the time was wasted. If classes began an hour later, students would be more awake, and I believe their grades and their mood would improve. Of course, there are practical problems. Parents who start work early may have difficulty taking their children to school, and sports practice would finish later in the evening. Still, I think these problems can be solved, and well-rested students are worth the effort.

listening.script: Here is my last question. Some schools have moved the start of the school day to a later hour so that teenagers can sleep longer. Do you think more schools should do this? Why or why not?
